docs.title: Welcome to ED3N Hydro Boards
docs.text:
Start growing smarter—without a tangle of breadboards or weeks of wiring. ED3N boards give everyone from weekend hobbyists to research labs a plug-and-play control platform for hydroponics.

Why we built them To make the first step into hydro automation as easy as stacking a HAT on a Pi—or, with our Pro board, skipping the Pi entirely.

docs.title: Board Line-up at a Glance
docs.text:
Board Core Idea Key Specs Best For ED3N Hydro Basic “Smart start” HAT • Raspberry Pi HAT• 1 × 12 V ⎓ in → 8 × 12 V / 12 W pump outputs• 8 × JST-PH I²C sensor ports Hobby growers • STEM classes • First prototypes ED3N Hydro Room to grow • All Basic features• Powers the Pi from the board• Extra I²C & power ports• Native Atlas Scientific EZO™ support Makers scaling up • Classroom research • Long-term projects ED3N Hydro Pro Standalone, rugged • Raspberry Pi Compute Module used• Industrial-grade parts, conformal coating• More JST expansion for future add-ons Commercial grows • Research labs • Harsh-env installs

(Full electrical specs are on each board’s page.)

docs.title: How to Get Started
docs.text:
1. Choose your board from the table above.
  2. Order on Amazon → search “ED3N Hydro Basic / Hydro / Pro” (listings live soon).
  3. Plug in pumps & sensors, follow the quick-start guide, and grow!

Boards arrive fully assembled, firmware-flashed, and electrically tested—no soldering required.

docs.title: Tested & Recommended Software
docs.text:
ED3N Hydro boards speak plain GPIO and I²C, so they work with any automation stack that can toggle pins and poll sensors. That said, the project began with one goal in mind:

“A plug-and-play board that shows off everything Mycodo can do.”

docs.title: Mycodo — flagship integration
docs.text:
Mycodo is an open-source environmental controller written for the Raspberry Pi. Kyle Gabriel (author) graciously helped ensure the ED3N pinout matches Mycodo’s dosing and sensor modules.

Why Mycodo pairs perfectly Details Native dosing Map each of the Hydro’s nine pump outputs to Mycodo’s “Doser” modules—set ml/min or ml/second directly. Sensor auto-detect Atlas EZO™ I²C addresses appear in the GUI; just choose pH, EC, etc., and Mycodo logs & graphs instantly. PID & scheduling Use built-in PID loops to maintain pH/EC, or create cron-style schedules for nutrient mixes. Dashboard & alerts Grafana dashboards out of the box; email/SMS/Telegram alerts when values drift.

docs.title: Quick-start with Mycodo
docs.text:
1. Flash Raspberry Pi OS Lite.
  2. Run the one-line installer from the Mycodo docs.
  3. Add Nine Doser outputs (GPIO 6, 13, 26, 16, 12, 5, 25, 24, 23).
  4. Add Sensor inputs for each Atlas EZO address (default 0x61, 0x62, …).
  5. Calibrate pumps (Mycodo Doser->Calibrate) and you’re ready to automate.

docs.title: Other stacks we’ve tested
docs.text:
Platform Notes Node-RED Use the rpi-gpio out node for pumps and i2c-bus contrib nodes for I²C sensors. Home Assistant GPIO control via the Raspberry Pi GPIO integration; sensor data over MQTT or I²C proxy scripts. Standalone Python Any library combo (e.g., RPi.GPIO + smbus2); see examples/ in the GitHub repo. Custom C / Rust Tested with pigpio C library and the rppal crate in Rust—rock-solid for industrial deployments.

(If you’ve validated another platform, open an Issue or PR and we’ll add it here.)

docs.title: Calibration reminder
docs.text:
Whatever software you choose, always:

  1. Prime each pump line.
  2. Run for a fixed time (e.g., 30 s).
  3. Measure the volume, repeat 3–5×, average, and store the ml/s rate.
  4. Re-calibrate after changing tubing, voltage, or fluid viscosity.

docs.title: Hydro Lite
docs.text:
A compact control board for automated hydroponic systems. It drives eight 12 V nutrient-dosing pumps plus one 12 V master pump, letting you pre-mix before filling the reservoir. No soldering is required—boards arrive fully assembled and electrically tested (sold on Amazon).

docs.title: Controlling the Pumps
docs.text:
Each MOSFET channel is wired to a dedicated Raspberry Pi GPIO pin. Set the pin HIGH to energise the MOSFET and run the pump; set it LOW to stop.

Connector label Pi GPIO Master Pump 6 Pump 1 13 Pump 2 26 Pump 3 16 Pump 4 12 Pump 5 5 Pump 6 25 Pump 7 24 Pump 8 23

docs.title: Calibration workflow
docs.text:
1. Prime each pump tubing with water or nutrient.
  2. In your control software (Python, Node-RED, etc.) turn one pump on for a known time — e.g. 30 seconds.
  3. Measure the volume dispensed (graduated cylinder works well).
  4. Repeat 3–5 times and average the results to spot any deviation.
  5. Enter that ml/sec (or ml/min) rate into your dosing algorithm.

Tip: Re-calibrate whenever you change tubing length, pump voltage, or fluid viscosity.

docs.title: Assembly & Test
docs.text:
Boards purchased on Amazon are pre-assembled and tested. For DIY assembly:

  1. Solder MCU, regulator, and passives.
  2. Apply 9 V; verify 3 .3 V rail.
  3. Flash Optiboot via the UPDI header.
  4. Run blink-pump.py to toggle each MOSFET and confirm outputs.

docs.text:
All-in-one controller with an on-board Raspberry Pi 5 Compute Module, three I²C buses (one dedicated to Atlas EZO™), and integrated isolated / non-isolated carrier footprints. Just plug in the EZO board, connect the probe or pump, and grow.

docs.title: Switching EZO™ boards from UART → I²C
docs.text:
1. Short the I²C pads on each board (https://www.instructables.com/UART-AND-I2C-MODE-SWITCHING-FOR-ATLAS-SCIENTIFIC-E/) – or use the \$13 I²C Toggler.

Note

Hydro Pro presents 8 JST + 10 Atlas = 18 physical ports. Keep ≤ 16 devices total for robust I²C signalling.

docs.text:
1. Short the I²C jumpers on each EZO board – Atlas guide: https://www.instructables.com/UART-AND-I2C-MODE-SWITCHING-FOR-ATLAS-SCIENTIFIC-E/

docs.title: I²C capacity & best practice
docs.text:
• Pi bus handles 16 devices reliably.
  • Hydro exposes 8 JST ports + 10 Atlas headers = 18 physical ports.
  • Populate up to 16 devices total (e.g., all 10 Atlas + 6 JST) to keep signal margins.

Note

Remove redundant consumer sensors as you migrate to Atlas probes to minimise bus load.

Use when sensors lack pull-ups or cable runs > 1 m. Extra pull-ups sit in parallel with existing ones.

Set GPIO HIGH → pump ON · LOW → pump OFF.

Calibration: run a pump for a fixed time (e.g. 30 s), measure volume, repeat 3–5×, average ml/s, and enter into your dosing software.
